extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in psychology and humor studies; general public interested in humor theory
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating humor with benign violation theory
extracted.subtask_description: Use the Benign Violation Theory to evaluate or design humorous stimuli by checking whether a situation (a) constitutes a violation, (b) is perceived as benign, and (c) produces those two perceptions simultaneously. The page summarizes the theory, types of violations, mechanisms that make violations seem benign, and boundary conditions when humor fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign Violation core conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor occurs when and only when three conditions are satisfied: (1) a situation is a violation, (2) the situation is benign, and (3) both perceptions occur simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central evaluative rule of the theory. Use it as a three-part checklist: identify if there is a perceived threat/wrongness (violation), whether that perception is accompanied by a sense that it is okay/safe/acceptable (benign), and whether both perceptions co-occur. The theory explains when things are and are not funny by reference to these three conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation (what counts as a violation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation refers to anything that threatens one's beliefs about how the world should be — something that seems threatening, unsettling, or wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include threats to physical well-being (e.g., tickling, play fighting), psychological well-being (e.g., insults, sarcasm), behaviors that break social norms (e.g., flatulence), cultural norm violations (e.g., unusual accents, scenes from Borat), linguistic norm violations (e.g., puns, malapropisms), logic norm violations (e.g., absurdities, non-sequiturs), and moral norm violations (e.g., disrespectful behavior, bestiality). When evaluating humor, identify which kind(s) of norm are being violated and whether the audience perceives them as a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived benignness (what makes a violation seem acceptable)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a violation to produce humor it also needs to be perceived as benign — it needs to seem okay, safe, or acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HuRL highlights three ways a violation can seem benign: (1) Alternative norms — e.g., one meaning of a phrase in a pun doesn’t make sense but an alternate meaning does; (2) Commitment to a violated norm — e.g., men may find sexist jokes funnier than women do because of differing commitments to the norm; (3) Psychological distance — e.g., 'comedy is tragedy plus time.' Psychological distance (temporal, spatial, social, hypothetical) often modulates whether a violation is seen as benign. When designing or judging jokes, assess which mechanism is making the violation benign for the target audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity and balance (boundary conditions where humor fails)
rubrics_metrics.description: The violation and benign perceptions must occur simultaneously and be balanced; if they do not co-occur or one predominates (too benign or too malign), humor will fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to diagnose failures: a situation can fail to be funny because it depicts a violation that does not simultaneously seem benign, or because it depicts a benign situation that has no violation. Examples: play fighting and tickling cease to elicit laughter when the attack stops (strictly benign) or becomes too aggressive (a malign violation). Jokes similarly fail when they are too tame (no perceived violation) or too risqué/harsh (not perceived as benign). Evaluators should check magnitude and timing: too little threat = no humor; too much = offense/distress rather than amusement.
